newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Bullish Russian shares set for new record.
newsitem.headline: Bullish Russian shares set for new record.

text.p: Russia's shares market looked set on Friday to best a record set only the previous day as new investment funds poured into the country in a scramble for stock that overlooked worries about President Boris Yeltsin's health.
Russian debt markets also firmed, benefiting from new New Year allocations to the emerging market, dealers said.

Moscow power company Mosenergo, which many foreign investors use as a proxy for the whole Russian market, touched $1.50 in afternoon trade then fell back to $1.38, after closing at $1.26 on Thursday. It has risen from below $1.00 at Christmas.

Another regional utility, Irkutskenergo, jumped 20 percent to $0.204 in mid-afternoon from Thursday's closing $0.170 after confirming it planned to issue American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) later this month.
ADRs allow foreign investors to buy shares while avoiding domestic settlement problems, and Russian companies which have issued ADRs have consistently outperformed the market.
Dealers across markets said funds were chasing a limited number of instruments but despite quick gains from low liquidity Russian stocks were a bargain.

"From a Western trading standpoint it looks extremely overdone," said a London-based equities dealer at a major Western bank. "But it's new money coming in and the (equities) market is still fairly cheap."

On Thursday the Russian Trading System 24-share index rose 1.6 percent to a record 231.48, as the market ignored news about Yeltsin sent to hospital with pneumonia on Wednesday. The index was only 189.41 on December 26.

Equity dealers and analysts said a correction was due after such strong gains, and could set in as early as late Friday. But many said the setback would be only five to 10 percent and quickly lead into a new rally.
"The market has gone up by 20 percent and we're probably going to stabilise at that," said Kristen Burton Steiner, deputy director of research at Alfa Capital.
"Stock is tight, and you have the new fund money which is drawing in new (investors') money, chasing it."

Financial analysts said there had been no major change in Russia's economic or financial situation, except for the illness of President Boris Yeltsin, who went to hospital on Wednesday and was diagnosed with pneumonia.
"It is the beginning of the new allocation year," said Burton Steiner, estimating that only about 25 percent of funds were from short-term speculators.
Other Russian markets also advanced.
Prices of longer term Treasury bills rose by half to a full point on Friday, levelling off in late trade after an early rise, traders said.

Dmitry Piskulov, chief dealer at ABN Amro in Moscow, said that Russian return on risk on domestic T-bills was still cheap when viewed internationally and that investors would continue to push prices up.
"There is still a lot of (uninvested) money," he said.
Dollar-denominated MinFin bonds, which are actively traded outside Russia, rose by up to about half a point as new funds poured into the market, following a rally in U.S. treasuries, dealers said.
"There's a lot of money flowing in," said the London-based trader. "It doesn't show signs of stopping any time soon."

The rouble, strictly controlled by the central bank, showed little movement, however. It was unchanged at 5,595 per dollar on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX) and eased in the interbank market to 5,599/5,600.
